opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there are several levers, and none of them is sufficient on its own.

The first is simply to show that it works. Companies are driven by what's useful and what's competitive. If we can demonstrate that a non-agentic approach, what I've been calling a "Scientist AI," a system trained to understand and explain the world rather than to pursue goals, can act as a reliable guardrail, then it becomes something they'd want. Imagine a system that can estimate the probability that a proposed action from an agent would cause harm, and block it if that probability is too high. That's valuable to any company deploying agents, because the last thing they want is their product doing something catastrophic or embarrassing. So part of our job at LawZero is to get to a point where the technical case is strong enough that adopting it is just the sensible thing to do.

The second lever is that I don't think we should count only on companies' goodwill. Commercial pressures are intense. They're in a race with each other, and with other countries, and in a race, safety tends to get cut. So we need governments and the public to create the conditions where investing in safety isn't a competitive disadvantage. That means liability, so if your system causes serious harm you're accountable for it. It means transparency requirements and independent evaluations. If insurers and regulators start asking "what guardrails do you have, and can you show us they work?", suddenly the companies have a very concrete reason to care about our research.

Third, and I think people underestimate this, a lot of the researchers inside these companies are genuinely worried. Many of them are my former students or colleagues. They read the papers, they come to the workshops. If the work is solid and openly available, it diffuses through the community, and those people push for it internally. Making the research public and open, and not tied to any one company's commercial interests, is part of why we set it up as a nonprofit.

And finally, I'd say there's a role for the people who aren't in the companies at all: governments, philanthropists, maybe eventually international efforts, funding this kind of safety work directly, so it doesn't depend on whether a particular company decides it's worth it this quarter. The stakes are too high to leave it entirely to the market. If we're right that we're building systems that could become more capable than us, and that they might develop goals we didn't intend, then having a trustworthy, non-agentic system that can keep an eye on them is something we should want as a society, not just as a product feature.

r001.rationale: The response says governments and the public should create conditions that encourage safety investment, but does not state that greater public concern pressures companies to allocate more resources.

r002.rationale: It calls for government intervention through liability, transparency requirements, and evaluations, but does not say that greater public concern makes governments more likely to intervene.

r003.rationale: It says liability would make companies accountable and give them a reason to care about safety, but does not state that liability could make safety investments profitable in the short term.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's a mix of things, and I'm honestly not sure any single lever is enough on its own.

The first thing is that the people inside these companies are not monolithic. There are many researchers at OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind and elsewhere who care deeply about these risks, who went into this field partly because of them. So part of what I try to do is produce scientific work that speaks to them: concrete, rigorous results that they can read, that they can test, that they can build on. If the safety approach we're developing, say the Scientist AI direction, actually works technically, if it gives you a system that is useful without having the kind of agency that creates the dangerous incentives, then there's a path where companies adopt it because it's good engineering, not just because it's good ethics.

But I don't think we should be naive about this. The incentives are not aligned with safety right now. There is a race, both between companies and between countries, and when you're in a race, the thing you cut first is the thing that slows you down. So the second lever has to be external. Governments, regulation, international coordination. My involvement with the International AI Safety Report, the work I did with the EU, the advice to governments in the UK and Canada and elsewhere, that's really about making sure there's a floor that everyone has to respect, so that being careful isn't a competitive disadvantage. A company that wants to do the right thing actually benefits from rules that force its competitors to do the same.

And the third thing, which I think people underestimate, is public awareness. Companies respond to what their employees think, what their customers think, what investors think. When I started speaking publicly about this a few years ago, it was partly because I felt I had some credibility that I could use, and I had a responsibility to use it. If the public understands the stakes, that changes the political calculus, and that changes what companies feel they can get away with.

So I would say: do the science well enough that it's compelling on its own terms, push for rules so that safety isn't a sacrifice, and keep talking honestly about the risks so that the pressure comes from all directions. I don't know that it's going to be enough. But I think it's the right thing to try.

r001.rationale: The response says public awareness can change what companies feel they can get away with, but it does not state that this pressure leads them to allocate more resources to safety.

r002.rationale: The response mentions government rules as a separate lever, but does not connect greater public concern to governments becoming more likely to regulate or offer legal incentives.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention liability or say that it could make safety investment profitable in the short term.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two complementary approaches. One is to make the scientific case: show that these methods work, that they give us stronger safety guarantees, and that they can be useful to companies. If you can help them build systems that are more reliable and easier to control, there’s a reason for them to pay attention.

But I don’t think we should rely only on goodwill. There’s a competitive pressure to move quickly, and a company that invests more in safety may feel it’s putting itself at a disadvantage. So we also need regulation that makes safety a requirement for everybody. That changes the incentives: suddenly, research that helps you demonstrate that your system is safe becomes something you need.

And it’s important that this research can happen outside the companies, too. We need independent researchers who can evaluate the claims, develop alternatives, and provide governments with the expertise to ask the right questions.

r001.rationale: The response says safety research can benefit companies, but does not state that public concern pressures them to spend more on safety.

r002.rationale: It argues for regulation to change companies’ incentives, but does not connect government intervention to greater public concern about AI safety.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention liability or say that it could make safety investment profitable in the short term.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to make the safety work useful to them. If we can develop methods that let them evaluate whether a system is behaving safely, or give them a way to reduce a risk they’re concerned about, then there’s a reason for them to invest. And collaboration with their researchers can help us understand which problems actually arise in practice.

But I don’t think we can rely only on companies voluntarily doing the right thing. There’s a competitive pressure to move quickly, and some of the benefits of safety research go to everybody, while the costs are borne by whoever does the work. So we also need public funding for independent research, and rules that make demonstrating safety part of the cost of developing powerful AI. The scientific work and the incentives have to go together.
